'''Louis Aub Bloomfield''' (born October 11, 1956) is a [[physics]] professor at the [[University of Virginia]]. Bloomfield became a [[fellow]] of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1994 for his work on [[cluster (physics)|cluster]] magnetism and has received several other significant honors. Bloomfield is often referenced as a physics authority in major news publications.

==Early life==
Bloomfield was born in [[Boston]], [[Massachusetts]] on October 11, 1956.<ref name="apsApker" /> He lived in [[Cleveland]], [[Ohio]] and [[Urbana, Illinois|Urbana]], [[Illinois]], graduating from [[Urbana High School (Illinois)|Urbana High School]] in 1974.<ref name="apsApker" /> Bloomfield attended [[Amherst College]], winning the [[LeRoy Apker Award]] in his [[Senior (education)|senior]] year.<ref name="apsApker">{{cite web |title=Where Are They Now? |url=https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/200011/where.cfm |website=American Physical Society |access-date=January 5, 2021}}</ref> He was most interested in medicine after graduating from Amherst, but his physics professors pressured him to apply to three prestigious physics programs in addition to taking the [[MCAT]] and applying to [[medical school]] at [[Johns Hopkins University]]. Bloomfield was accepted into all three physics programs and medical school, but decided to go into physics after asking himself whether he really wanted to be "cutting apart dead bodies in Baltimore."<ref name="apsApker" /> Bloomfield attended [[Stanford University]] for physics, receiving his [[Ph.D.]] from the school in 1983. He began teaching at the [[University of Virginia]] two years later after a [[postdoc]] at [[Bell Laboratories]].<ref name="biography">{{cite web |title=How Things Work |url=http://www4.hcmut.edu.vn/~huynhqlinh/olympicvl/tailieu/web/How_things_work/biography.html |access-date=January 5, 2021}}</ref>

==Career==
Bloomfield began teaching physics at the University of Virginia in 1985.<ref name="apsApker"/> He developed and began teaching a course entitled "How Things Work" in 1991, which he has since taught to thousands of students. This course's success, along with the publishing of a textbook on the subject under the same title, has led to Bloomfield doing a number of interviews and explanations as a guest for large news companies. Bloomfield's explanations of everyday activities and questions have been featured in ''[[USA Today]]'', ''[[The Huffington Post]]'', and ''[[The Washington Post]]'', where he did a series of explanations on sports during the [[2016 Summer Olympics]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Rossman |first1=Sean |title=What would happen if you were hit by a penny falling from a skyscraper? |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation-now/2017/03/15/what-would-happen-if-you-were-hit-penny-falling-skyscraper/99160982/ |website=USA TODAY |access-date=January 5, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Wolchover |first1=Natalie |title=Could Penny Kill You If It Were Dropped From Skyscraper? |url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/could-penny-kill-you_n_1321721 |website=HuffPost |date=5 March 2012 |access-date=January 5, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Payne |first1=Marissa |title=Why Olympic swimmers wear two caps in the pool |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/early-lead/wp/2016/08/09/why-olympic-swimmers-wear-two-caps-in-the-pool/ |newspaper=The Washington Post |access-date=January 5, 2020}}</ref> Bloomfield worked with UVA to create an instructional video on [[social distancing]] during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Newman |first1=Caroline |title=Physics Professor Lou Bloomfield Explains the Crucial Math Behind Social Distancing |url=https://archive.news.virginia.edu/content/physics-professor-lou-bloomfield-explains-crucial-math-behind-social-distancing/ |website=UVA Today |access-date=January 5, 2020 |language=en |date=15 March 2020}}</ref>

===Inventions===
Bloomfield has expertise in the field of [[borosilicate materials]] and has developed multiple products using this technology. Borosilicates are [[Viscoelasticity|viscoelastic]] (a [[portmanteau]] of "[[viscous]]" and "[[Elasticity (physics)|elastic]]"), a property that is useful in multiple areas.<ref>{{cite web |title=Lou Bloomfield: The Invention of Vistik: Physics professor invents a new substance |url=https://uvamagazine.org/videos/lou_bloomfield_the_invention_of_vistik |website=Virginia Magazine |access-date=January 5, 2020 |language=en}}</ref> These inventions include Vistik, a material designed for use in stabilizing wobbly tables, and EarJellies, which are earplugs made from a similar material.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Samarrai |first1=Fariss |title=U.Va. Physicist Bloomfield Develops New Silicone Rubber |url=https://news.virginia.edu/content/uva-physicist-bloomfield-develops-new-silicone-rubber |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130303015927/http://news.virginia.edu/content/uva-physicist-bloomfield-develops-new-silicone-rubber |url-status=dead |archive-date=March 3, 2013 |website=UVA Today |access-date=January 5, 2020 |language=en |date=27 February 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Samarrai |first1=Fariss |title=Listen Up! This UVA Professor Has Invented a Better Earplug |url=https://archive.news.virginia.edu/content/listen-uva-professor-has-invented-better-earplug/ |website=UVA Today |access-date=January 5, 2020 |language=en |date=9 February 2018}}</ref>
